transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi Dr. Smith. Um... I guess what brings me in is... well, it's a whole situation with my job. They kind of told me I had to come see somebody. 

See, I work as a personal care aide, and it's a really demanding job, you know? You're on your feet all day, lifting people, and you have to be so careful because if somebody goes down, it's on you. So we have these staff meetings—usually on Tuesday mornings in this cramped little breakroom with these buzzing fluorescent lights—and the supervisor was just droning on about safety protocols, not even explaining the mechanics of it right. And I just... I got really, really worked up about it. Because it's life or death for these clients! 

So I got up right there in the meeting, and I started acting out this whole fall-prevention drill to show them how it actually happens. I grabbed a couple of those plastic folding chairs to represent the bed and the commode, and I was waving my arms all around, trying to demonstrate how you gotta block the hips, how you gotta pivot and catch their center of gravity. I was really getting into it, showing the exact angles, my arms just going everywhere. 

And I guess I was making a scene, because the supervisor and a couple of the other folks started telling me to sit down. They were like, "Okay, we get it, sit down now." But the thing is... I couldn't. I just couldn't seem to stop, even when they kept telling me to. I was still moving the chairs around and waving my arms and explaining the pivot, like I just had to get the whole routine out of my system and I couldn't turn it off. They got real weird about it after that, and... well, here I am.
Over the past week or so, have you noticed that you're needing a lot less sleep than usual but still feel full of energy and drive the next day?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask about sleep, because... actually, yes. It's been exactly like that. The last week, maybe ten days? I haven't really been sleeping much at all. But I don't feel tired! That's the crazy part. 

Like, normally, if I don't get my solid seven hours, I'm dragging at work, right? Especially with all the lifting. But lately... I'll go to bed around midnight, maybe one in the morning, because I'm just so wired thinking about all the things I need to do. And then, boom. It's 3:00 AM, maybe 3:30, and my eyes just snap open. And I'm not just awake, Dr. Smith, I am *awake*. I feel completely refreshed, like I just slept for ten hours. 

So I get up, and the whole house is pitch black, quiet as a tomb, you know? And I just feel this... this incredible surge of energy. Like I'm ready to tackle the entire day before the sun even comes up. I'll sit at the kitchen table with just the little stove light on, and I'll start making all these plans. I've been writing out these entirely new, super-detailed safety protocols for the clinic—pages and pages of them, diagramming the exact body mechanics, the physics of a fall, everything the supervisor got wrong. 

And it doesn't even cross my mind that it's weird to be doing this at three in the morning! I just feel so driven, so clear-headed. I'll be sitting there in the dark, scribbling away, feeling like I'm finally figuring out all the solutions to these massive problems. And then I go into work a few hours later, and I still have all that energy. I don't even need coffee. I just feel... I don't know, dialed in. Like two or three hours of sleep is suddenly all my body needs to run at 100 percent.

Have you ever had a period in the past—lasting a week or more—where you felt this same kind of high energy and reduced need for sleep, or on the other hand, a stretch of time where you felt unusually depressed, low, or lost interest in things?

Well, it's funny you ask about the past, because... yes, actually. Yes. This whole thing—this feeling of just being completely wired, running on fumes but feeling like a million bucks, staying up all night making these massive, intricate plans—it's not just a one-time thing. It's been happening on and off for... gosh, I'd say about 11 months now. Almost a full year of this back-and-forth. 

I remember the first time it really hit me, it was last fall. The leaves were just starting to turn that rusty orange color, and I was working the overnight shift at this other facility—a real rundown place, smelled like industrial bleach and old soup. And I just stopped sleeping. Like, completely. I'd do my shift, come home at 7:00 AM, and instead of going to bed, I'd start tearing apart my entire apartment to reorganize the kitchen cabinets based on the exact frequency I used each utensil. I was convinced I had found the perfect system for efficiency, you know? I stayed up for days, just buzzing, feeling like I was the only one who really understood how things should work.

And then it would fade out, and I'd go back to normal for a bit, but then a few months later, boom—it would happen again. Another stretch of just... endless energy. I'd be up at all hours, drafting these huge proposals for the clinic, or deciding I was going to learn to speak fluent Russian in a week. I bought all these books, downloaded all these apps. I didn't even sleep, I just listened to Russian vocabulary tapes in the dark until the sun came up. 

So yeah, these stretches where I'm just too energized, barely sleeping at all, pushing these huge, grand plans... they've definitely been coming and going for about 11 months now. It's like a switch flips, and suddenly I'm running at warp speed, and I just can't turn it off until it decides to turn itself off.

During these periods of high energy and racing plans, have you ever seen, heard, or believed things that other people told you weren't real or didn't make sense—like hearing voices or feeling certain you had special powers or a special mission?

Well... yeah. Yeah, actually, it's kind of wild that you bring that up. Because when I was in those really fired-up stretches I was just talking about, you know, where I'm sleeping only a few hours and making these big plans for the clinic... things do get a little strange. 

Like, I'd be sitting there at my kitchen table at 3:30 in the morning, right? The whole neighborhood is dead silent, not even a car driving by outside. And I will hear, clear as day, these calls. Just... hearing calls that absolutely weren't there. Sometimes it sounded like one of the heavy-assist clients from the facility yelling out from another room, or sometimes it was just a voice calling my name from down my own hallway. I'd actually get up from my papers, walk all the way down the hall, check the front door, check the deadbolt, because it sounded so incredibly real. I'd be looking around in the dark, but... there was never anybody there. Just empty air and the refrigerator humming.

And then, while all that's going on, I also started getting this intense... well, more than a feeling, really, a total certainty about my supervisor. The one who runs those awful Tuesday meetings. I was feeling absolutely sure that my supervisor was setting traps for me. I'd go into work for my shift, still buzzing with all this energy from the night before, and I'd see a wet floor sign moved two inches to the left, or a gait belt left draped over a commode at a weird angle, and I just knew she had placed it there specifically to trip me up. To test my safety awareness or catch me slipping so she could ruin me and get me fired. 

I'd spend half my shift documenting every single thing she did, writing it down in this little spiral notebook I kept in my scrub pocket, because I felt like I had to stay one step ahead of her traps at all times. The other aides told me I was overthinking it, that she was just a sloppy manager and it didn't mean anything, but they just couldn't see how it was all connected like I could. I just knew she was orchestrating the whole thing to mess with my head while I was trying to fix the place.

When these high-energy stretches end and your mood and sleep go back to normal, do the voices or the strong suspicions about your supervisor go away completely, or do they sometimes continue even when you're feeling like your usual self?

Well, see, that's the thing that really gets under my skin about all this. You'd think that once the engine finally cools down and I go back to sleeping a regular seven or eight hours, you know, when I stop staying up all night and all that... you'd think the rest of it would just pack up and leave, too. But it doesn't. 

Like, there was this one calmer stretch a while back. I was finally sleeping more normally, going to bed at a decent hour instead of midnight or three in the morning. I wasn't rushing around with all those massive projects anymore. I'd come home from the facility, watch a little TV, maybe eat a regular dinner—just a frozen Salisbury steak or something, nothing fancy, no intricate meal planning or reorganizing the kitchen—and just relax. I felt totally fine. My mood was level, my energy was just... average, everyday energy. 

But even then, during that whole time, for several weeks I still heard my name being called. I'd be sitting on my couch, totally relaxed, watching a baseball game, and I'd hear it from the hallway. Just my name, clear as a bell, or someone saying "Hey!" from right right behind my shoulder. 

And at work? Man, even though I wasn't buzzing with all that warp-speed energy anymore, I stayed absolutely convinced that people at work were keeping notes on me. I'd be doing my regular rounds, helping Mr. Henderson with his transfer board, just doing my normal everyday routine, and I'd see the supervisor or even the other aides holding a clipboard or glancing my way, and I just knew they were documenting my every move. I wasn't fired up or trying to outsmart them with my own spiral notebooks anymore because I was just feeling like my usual self, but I still knew they were doing it. It lasted for weeks like that. I'd check the breakroom, check the nurses' station when they walked away, trying to catch them slipping those secret notes into my personnel file. 

So yeah, the energy goes away, the sleep comes back, the grand plans stop... but that feeling of them tracking me and the voices calling out to me? It sticks around. It just hangs on like a bad cold for weeks on end, even when everything else is quiet.
